screens.title: Packaging, Deployment, and Project Archiving
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging is the step that converts everything you built in the editor into a standalone application players can run. In practice, packaging compiles code, cooks assets for a platform, and removes editor-only files so the result is focused and efficient. This matters because a packaged build is what testers, players, and stores receive — differences between the editor and a packaged game can reveal runtime-only issues like missing assets or platform SDK problems. In this chapter you will learn how to set essential project settings, choose appropriate build configuration for testing versus release, start a package for Windows, and monitor the engine during cooking. You will also learn how to read the output log to find errors, and how to approach common failures and large package sizes. Finally, you will see the recommended practices for keeping long-term archives small and restorable. By the end of the lesson you will understand not just the menu clicks, but why each packaging choice matters and how to diagnose the most common problems that block a successful build. Ready to prepare your project for the next step? Let's get started with the settings that control what actually gets included.

screens.title: What Packaging Does and Why "Cooking" Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging is the process that turns your editor project into a standalone application. At its core it compiles code, cooks assets for the chosen platform, and removes editor-only data so the output contains only what the game needs to run. 'Cooking' specifically converts assets into platform-ready formats — for example converting textures and shaders so they will load efficiently on Windows or mobile devices. Using a pak file bundles content into a single archive which simplifies distribution and can improve load performance. A common mistake is to assume that what runs in the editor will always run identically when packaged; editor runtime and packaged runtime differ because cooking can reveal missing references, and shipping configuration strips debug helpers. A concrete example: if a level is not added to the packaging map list, it may load fine in the editor but crash the packaged executable when the game tries to open it. Another misconception is believing pak files are optional for small projects — for distribution and efficient loading pak files are recommended. Takeaway: packaging prepares assets and code for runtime; cooking and pak files determine what is actually included and how efficiently it can run.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › What Packaging Does
Packaging, Cooking, and Pak Files
A precise definition and the practical effects you must check before shipping.
What packaging does
Compiles code, gathers and cooks assets, strips editor files, and produces a runnable folder or package for the platform.
What cooking means
Converting assets into platform-specific formats so they load correctly in the packaged runtime.
Pak files
Single-file content archives that improve distribution and often loading performance.
Key Takeaway

Treat packaging as a conversion step: if something works only in the editor, expect to test the packaged build and check cooked assets and included maps.

Illustrative Example
A map that is playable in the editor but not listed under packaging will be omitted and can cause a crash when loaded by the packaged game.
Concrete Scenario
You test a level in the editor, forget to add it to the packaging map list, package, and the packaged exe crashes on level load. The fix is to add the map then repackage or include it in the cooking list.
Common Misconception
Believing Development and Shipping builds behave identically. Development builds include debug info and may hide some shipping-only runtime failures.
Check
Verify cooked assets and pak file contents after packaging to ensure critical content is present.

screens.title: Configure Project Settings for Packaging
screens.narratorSegment: Successful packaging begins with the Project Settings. Start by setting your default maps: Editor Startup Map, Game Default Map, and any transition maps your game uses. Then open the Packaging section and confirm the 'List of maps to include in a packaged build' explicitly lists every level the game may load at runtime. Missing a map here is a common root cause of packaged crashes. In Packaging options choose Build Configuration. Use Development builds for debugging because they include symbols and extra logging; switch to Shipping for final releases because it strips debug helpers and optimizes size. Enable 'Use Pak File' to bundle game content and consider 'Cook everything in the project' for a clean, predictable cook. 'Full Rebuild' is useful if you encounter corrupted assets or strange packaging errors. Finally, under Platforms check that the target platform is enabled and platform-specific SDK paths are set for mobile builds. A concrete example: if you plan to package for Android, confirm the Android SDK and NDK paths are configured so the package step can complete. Misconception to avoid: toggling everything on is not safer; enable only what you need and verify each change with a small test package. Takeaway: project settings are the contract that defines what the packaged build will contain; set them deliberately and verify.

screens.title: Initiating a Package and Monitoring the Cook
screens.narratorSegment: Packaging starts with the menu command: File, Package Project, then choose your target platform such as Windows (64-bit). When prompted, select an output directory. The engine then begins cooking assets, compiling code, and building a distributable folder. Cooking can be time-consuming depending on project size. While the package runs, open the Output Log window in the editor to follow progress messages, warnings, and errors. The Output Log provides step-by-step feedback; red error lines often show missing assets, failed Blueprint compilation, or SDK problems. If packaging fails immediately, inspect the log for errors like missing default maps or Blueprint compile errors that slipped by in Play-In-Editor. If the package completes but the executable crashes, check the Saved/Logs folder inside the packaged build for runtime logs. A concrete example: starting a Windows 64-bit package for a demo level can take minutes; if the Output Log shows a missing asset during cooking, you can stop, add the missing map or fix the Blueprint, and try again. Misconception: watching the progress bar alone is not enough; the Output Log contains the detailed clues you need. Takeaway: run small test packages first, watch the Output Log, and use packaged logs for post-launch crashes.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Initiate & Monitor Packaging
Packaging Steps
A compact step-by-step checklist to follow during a package run.
1. Select File → Package Project → Platform
Pick the target platform such as Windows (64-bit).
2. Choose output directory
Create a dedicated folder like MyGame_Packaged to keep outputs organized.
3. Monitor cooking and compile steps
Open Window → Developer Tools → Output Log to follow detailed messages.
Pro Tip

Run a short test package of a small map first to validate settings before a full project package.

What the Output Log reveals
  • Red errors indicate failures that must be resolved before a successful package.
  • Warnings can point to missing references or deprecated assets to review.
  • Success messages confirm cooked assets and compiled binaries were produced.
Example
If Output Log shows 'Missing map' during cooking, add the map to the packaging list and re-run packaging. If packaging completes but exe crashes, open the packaged Saved/Logs folder to read the runtime log.

screens.title: Common Packaging Failures and Initial Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When packaging fails or a packaged game crashes, you can narrow the cause by checking a few reliable places. If packaging fails immediately, open the editor Output Log and look for red error lines; common causes include missing default maps, unresolved Blueprint compilation errors, and missing mobile SDKs. If the packaged executable crashes at launch, inspect the game's Saved/Logs folder inside the packaged output for detailed runtime logs that show the call stack and missing assets. For missing maps, confirm your 'List of maps to include in a packaged build' contains every map the game may load. For Blueprint errors, open each Blueprint and run a full compile in the editor — some runtime-only problems only show up when cooked so also try a Development build to get richer logs. For SDK issues on mobile, verify platform SDK paths are correct in Project Settings. A typical quick recovery sequence: check Output Log, fix the first red error, perform a Full Rebuild in Packaging options if assets seem corrupted, then repackage. Misconception: assuming a successful editor test guarantees a working packaged build — always validate using the packaged logs. Closing question: after you find an error in the Output Log, what single change will you test first?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Common Failures & Troubleshooting
Common Failures
A side-by-side comparison of symptoms and first actions.
Packaging fails immediately
Check Output Log for red errors: missing maps, Blueprint compile errors, or missing SDKs. Fix the earliest error and try again.
Packaged exe crashes on launch
Open Saved/Logs in the packaged folder to inspect runtime logs and stack traces for missing assets or runtime exceptions.
Large package size
Review assets for high-resolution textures or uncompressed audio; confirm you enabled pak files and did not accidentally include large editor-only files.
Quick Recovery Steps
  1. Open Output Log; locate the first red error and resolve it in the editor.
  2. Run a Development build to gather richer logs or reproduce the crash locally.
  3. If assets appear corrupted, enable Full Rebuild and repackage to regenerate cooked content.
  4. For missing maps, add them to the packaging list and re-run the package.
Example Troubleshoot
Output Log shows a failed Blueprint compile during cooking. Open the Blueprint, compile, fix errors, and repackage. If the packaged game still crashes, check the packaged Saved/Logs for runtime stack traces.
A systematic approach—fix the first error, repackage, and repeat—saves time and avoids chasing misleading symptoms.

screens.title: Deployment Considerations for Windows and Mobile
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment varies by target platform. For Windows, the packaged output is a folder containing an executable and associated content; you typically compress that folder into a zip for distribution or provide an installer. Before distributing, test the executable on a clean machine to confirm dependencies are present. For mobile platforms, packaging produces platform-specific bundles such as an APK for Android or an IPA for iOS; these require additional configuration for SDK paths and signing credentials. A clear example: packaging an Android build fails if the Android SDK or NDK paths are not set in Project Settings. Another area to watch is the difference between Development and Shipping builds: Development builds are larger and include debug helpers, so they are useful for diagnosing crashes on device, while Shipping builds must be signed and may require store compliance steps. A common misconception is assuming packaging is the same as deployment — packaging creates the build; deployment is the act of delivering it to users and often requires zipping, signing, or uploading to a store. Takeaway: test packaged builds on the target hardware and verify SDK and signing settings for mobile before attempting distribution.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Deployment Considerations
Target Platform Differences
Understand how output format and signing affect deployment.
Windows
Produces an exe and content folder. Zip for distribution and test on a clean machine to confirm dependencies.
Android / iOS
Produces APK or IPA and requires SDK/NDK paths, signing credentials, and store-specific upload steps.
Build Type
Use Development to debug on device, Shipping for optimized release builds that must be signed before submission.
Practical Checklist
  • Verify platform SDKs and signing settings are configured in Project Settings.
  • Package a Development build to test on device; gather logs if crashes occur.
  • For distribution, switch to Shipping and follow store signing requirements.
Example
Android packaging will fail without Android SDK paths. Confirm paths and test the resulting APK on a physical device before submitting to testers or stores.
Remember: packaging prepares the build; deployment requires additional platform steps such as signing, zipping, or uploading to stores.

screens.title: Why Archive a Project? Purpose and Principles
screens.narratorSegment: Archiving is the practice of creating a complete, restorable snapshot of your Unreal project for long-term storage or milestone sign-off. Unlike daily version control commits that record diffs, an archive bundles everything needed to reopen and run the project later — including files you may not track in Git. A good archive captures project assets, configuration, and any local engine builds or platform-specific settings. This matters because team members, future you, or release QA may need an exact restore point that is independent from a commit history. A concrete example: you finish a vertical slice for a prototype milestone. Creating an archive ensures you can reproduce performance tests months later even if branch histories are pruned. Two common misconceptions are worth addressing. First, some people assume Git is sufficient for long-term snapshots; Git stores tracked files but typically omits large binaries and temporary build artifacts that you may still want restored. Second, an archive is not just a zip of everything — cleaning out temporary folders before archiving reduces size and avoids leaking machine-specific caches. As a result, treat version control as your primary collaboration tool and archives as periodic, complete backups that you can hand to QA or store offline. How would you name and date your next archive so it’s clearly retrievable?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Why Archive a Project?
Definition

An archive is a complete compressed snapshot of the project folder, cleaned of temporary files so it can be restored later without depending solely on version control.

What an archive should include
  • Content and Config folders (Content/, Config/)
  • Project source files and any third-party assets you own
  • Platform-specific settings or local engine builds if necessary
Use descriptive names and dates
Why it matters

A clean archive ensures reproducible builds, aids QA handoffs, and preserves a restorable snapshot independent of your repository's state.

Analogy

Think of an archive like a packaged time capsule: it contains everything needed to reopen the project at that exact moment, cleaned of temporary caches.

Quick checklist
  • Confirm maps and packaged build run as expected
  • Close the Editor before deleting temporary folders
  • Delete Binaries, Build, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache, Saved
  • Compress the cleaned project folder with a clear name and date

screens.title: Cleaning a Project Before Archiving
screens.narratorSegment: Cleaning a project before archiving reduces file size and removes machine-specific caches that can be regenerated. The essential directories to remove are Binaries, Build, Intermediate, DerivedDataCache, and Saved. Always close the Unreal Editor before deleting these folders to avoid corrupting files. A typical workflow is: first verify your packaged build runs and that all maps are included. Then, copy the project folder to a staging location. From that staging copy, delete the five temporary directories. Deleting these does not remove core content or assets tracked in source control; it removes compiled binaries, cached shaders, and autosave data. Next, compress the cleaned folder into a single archive file, using a clear name like ProjectName_Milestone-YYYYMMDD. zip. Store the archive on an external drive or cloud storage and record its checksum and metadata. One practical example: before delivering a milestone, a developer removes the temporary folders, zips the folder, and uploads it to a shared archive bucket. Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Cleaning Before Archive
Step-by-step
  1. Confirm your packaged build runs and default map loads.
  2. Close Unreal Editor to avoid locked files.
  3. Make a staging copy of the project folder.
  4. Delete: Binaries, Build, DerivedDataCache, Intermediate, Saved.
  5. Compress the cleaned folder to .zip or .7z with date-stamped name.
Common mistake

Deleting files while the editor is open can corrupt caches or leave partial deletes. Always close the editor first.

Paths you can safely remove
ProjectRoot/ Binaries/
ProjectRoot/ Build/
ProjectRoot/ DerivedDataCache/
ProjectRoot/ Intermediate/
ProjectRoot/ Saved/
These are regenerable by the editor and reduce archive size dramatically.
Final steps
  • Compress and verify archive checksum.
  • Store at least one copy offsite or on an external drive.
  • Record name, date, engine version, and included platform builds.

screens.title: Backup Strategies and Scheduling
screens.narratorSegment: A backup strategy reduces risk and ensures you can recover from data loss, corruption, or an accidental commit. Start by choosing frequency: daily lightweight backups for active development, weekly full archives for milestones, and monthly or milestone archives for long-term storage. Use multiple storage targets: an on-site external drive for fast restore, and a cloud archive for offsite safety. Name each backup clearly with project name, milestone, and date. A practical schedule: perform daily incremental backups to cloud storage and create a full cleaned archive at every major milestone or release candidate. Keep at least two historical copies so you can roll back if a recent archive is corrupted. Validate your backups by occasionally restoring an archive to a test machine — a backup that is never restored may be unusable when needed. Another useful practice is to include a small metadata text file inside each archive that lists engine version, included platforms, and key packaging settings used, so future restores know how to regenerate caches. A common misconception is that cloud storage alone is enough. Combine local and offsite storage for speed and redundancy. Finally, automate where possible: use scheduled scripts or backup tools to avoid human error and maintain a consistent cadence. This disciplined approach protects months of work and avoids last-minute scramble before a release.

screens.title: Reading Packaged Build Logs and Diagnosing Crashes
screens.narratorSegment: When a packaged game crashes on startup, the most important artifact to inspect is the packaged build's log file. These live in the packaged folder under Saved/Logs, for example MyGame/Windows/MyGame/Saved/Logs/MyGame. log. Open the most recent log and search for 'Error' or 'Exception' lines and call stacks that indicate missing assets, failed loads, or plugin initialization errors. A concrete example: a packaged game crashes after a missing level reference; the log will show a failed load for a map or asset path and the engine call stack. If the packaged log is sparse, consider packaging a Development build first — Development packages include more diagnostic output and symbol information that makes the log easier to interpret. Another common check is to compare the editor Output Log to the packaged log; differences often reveal runtime-only issues such as cook-time excluded maps or assets not listed for packaging. For mobile targets, missing SDKs or signing issues produce distinctive messages you can search for. Remember to test on target hardware because behavior can differ from the editor. Finally, reproduce the crash with a Development package, inspect the log for the root cause, fix the asset or Blueprint, and then create a clean Shipping package for distribution. A useful habit is to keep a brief checklist when a crash occurs: check Saved/Logs, test Development build, verify included maps, and search for missing plugins. Which log entry would you investigate first on your next crash?

screens.title: Hands-on Checklist: Package, Test, Archive
screens.narratorSegment: Use a repeatable checklist when packaging and archiving to avoid last-minute problems. Start by confirming your Default Maps and Packaging list include the intended levels. For an initial test package set Build Configuration to Development and check Use Pak File; don’t mark For Distribution for testing. Choose File > Package Project > Windows > Windows (64-bit), select a clean output folder, and monitor the Output Log during cooking for obvious errors. After packaging, navigate into the packaged folder and test the executable on your target machine or a test VM. If the game crashes, inspect the packaged Saved/Logs directory for the game's log file and reproduce with a Development build for more detail. Once the build behaves, close the editor and create a staging copy of the project for archiving. Delete Binaries, Build, DerivedDataCache, Intermediate, and Saved from the staging copy, compress the folder into a dated archive, and store it in your backup locations. As an assessment-style check, ask yourself two questions: where would you find the packaged log if the exe crashes, and which five folders are safe to delete before zipping the project? Keeping a written checklist and automation scripts for repeated tasks will save time and reduce errors. Try this checklist now with your demo level and confirm you can both launch the packaged exe and produce a clean archive that restores correctly.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Packaging Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three compact concepts to anchor your understanding of packaging. Packaging compiles and bundles assets, Blueprints, and code into a standalone application suitable for distribution. Cooking prepares assets for the target platform, converting them into optimized formats before packaging and reducing runtime surprises. The Pak file is a single archive that groups game content for efficient distribution and loading. Keep these concepts in mind because they explain why packaging settings and the list of included maps are both critical to a working build. If a map isn’t listed or an asset fails to cook, the packaged game may crash at runtime. These three terms are quick checks when something goes wrong: Did you cook? Did you include the maps? Did you use a Pak file for distribution? Key Concepts — Packaging Basics means packaging, cooking, and pak files are the foundational terms that determine whether a build runs as expected.. In practical terms, three core ideas to hold on to. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Packaging is the step that converts everything you built in the editor into a standalone application players can run. In practice, packaging compiles code, cooks assets for a platform, and removes editor-only files so the result is focused and efficient. This matters because a packaged build is what testers, players, and stores receive — differences between the editor and a packaged game can reveal runtime-only issues like missing assets or platform SDK problems. In this chapter you will learn how to set essential project settings, choose appropriate build configuration for testing versus release, start a package for Windows, and monitor the engine during cooking. You will also learn how to read the output log to find errors, and how to approach common failures and large package sizes. Finally, you will see the recommended practices for keeping long-term archives small and restorable. By the end of the lesson you will understand not just the menu clicks, but why each packaging choice matters and how to diagnose the most common problems that block a successful build. Ready to prepare your project for the next step? Let's get started with the settings that control what actually gets included.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure project settings needed for packaging, run the packaging pipeline for a target platform, and begin troubleshooting common packaging errors. You will learn to set default maps so the packaged game launches reliably, choose a build configuration appropriate for testing or releasing, and enable the packaging options that control asset cooking and pak file creation. You'll also gain practical skills in reading the Output Log inside the editor and the runtime logs produced by a packaged build, which are critical for diagnosing crashes that only appear after packaging. Finally, you will understand the purpose of full rebuilds and cooked assets and how they reduce mysterious runtime failures. Each objective pairs a concrete action — for example, packaging a Windows 64-bit build — with why it matters, like ensuring the executable contains all required maps and cooked content. These skills let you move from editor testing to delivering playable builds to testers or players with confidence.

These objectives focus on hands-on actions: checking maps, adjusting packaging options, initiating a package, and interpreting logs. First, you'll learn to confirm the Editor Startup Map and Game Default Map are correct so the packaged executable opens the intended level. Next, you'll configure packaging options such as Build Configuration, Use Pak File, and Cook settings so the output matches testing or distribution needs. Then you'll actually run File, Package Project, choose Windows 64-bit, and pick an output folder, learning to watch the cooking and compilation steps. Lastly, you'll practice reading the Output Log and the packaged game's Saved Logs to find errors and decide whether to run a full rebuild or switch to a development build for more debugging detail. Each objective is paired with a short verification task so you can be confident the setting change had the intended effect. These practical skills make it possible to move from an editor prototype to a testable build and to respond quickly when packaging fails.

Packaging is the process that turns your editor project into a standalone application. At its core it compiles code, cooks assets for the chosen platform, and removes editor-only data so the output contains only what the game needs to run. 'Cooking' specifically converts assets into platform-ready formats — for example converting textures and shaders so they will load efficiently on Windows or mobile devices. Using a pak file bundles content into a single archive which simplifies distribution and can improve load performance. A common mistake is to assume that what runs in the editor will always run identically when packaged; editor runtime and packaged runtime differ because cooking can reveal missing references, and shipping configuration strips debug helpers. A concrete example: if a level is not added to the packaging map list, it may load fine in the editor but crash the packaged executable when the game tries to open it. Another misconception is believing pak files are optional for small projects — for distribution and efficient loading pak files are recommended. Takeaway: packaging prepares assets and code for runtime; cooking and pak files determine what is actually included and how efficiently it can run.

Successful packaging begins with the Project Settings. Start by setting your default maps: Editor Startup Map, Game Default Map, and any transition maps your game uses. Then open the Packaging section and confirm the 'List of maps to include in a packaged build' explicitly lists every level the game may load at runtime. Missing a map here is a common root cause of packaged crashes. In Packaging options choose Build Configuration. Use Development builds for debugging because they include symbols and extra logging; switch to Shipping for final releases because it strips debug helpers and optimizes size. Enable 'Use Pak File' to bundle game content and consider 'Cook everything in the project' for a clean, predictable cook. 'Full Rebuild' is useful if you encounter corrupted assets or strange packaging errors. Finally, under Platforms check that the target platform is enabled and platform-specific SDK paths are set for mobile builds. A concrete example: if you plan to package for Android, confirm the Android SDK and NDK paths are configured so the package step can complete. Misconception to avoid: toggling everything on is not safer; enable only what you need and verify each change with a small test package. Takeaway: project settings are the contract that defines what the packaged build will contain; set them deliberately and verify.

Packaging starts with the menu command: File, Package Project, then choose your target platform such as Windows (64-bit). When prompted, select an output directory. The engine then begins cooking assets, compiling code, and building a distributable folder. Cooking can be time-consuming depending on project size. While the package runs, open the Output Log window in the editor to follow progress messages, warnings, and errors. The Output Log provides step-by-step feedback; red error lines often show missing assets, failed Blueprint compilation, or SDK problems. If packaging fails immediately, inspect the log for errors like missing default maps or Blueprint compile errors that slipped by in Play-In-Editor. If the package completes but the executable crashes, check the Saved/Logs folder inside the packaged build for runtime logs. A concrete example: starting a Windows 64-bit package for a demo level can take minutes; if the Output Log shows a missing asset during cooking, you can stop, add the missing map or fix the Blueprint, and try again. Misconception: watching the progress bar alone is not enough; the Output Log contains the detailed clues you need. Takeaway: run small test packages first, watch the Output Log, and use packaged logs for post-launch crashes.

When packaging fails or a packaged game crashes, you can narrow the cause by checking a few reliable places. If packaging fails immediately, open the editor Output Log and look for red error lines; common causes include missing default maps, unresolved Blueprint compilation errors, and missing mobile SDKs. If the packaged executable crashes at launch, inspect the game's Saved/Logs folder inside the packaged output for detailed runtime logs that show the call stack and missing assets. For missing maps, confirm your 'List of maps to include in a packaged build' contains every map the game may load. For Blueprint errors, open each Blueprint and run a full compile in the editor — some runtime-only problems only show up when cooked so also try a Development build to get richer logs. For SDK issues on mobile, verify platform SDK paths are correct in Project Settings. A typical quick recovery sequence: check Output Log, fix the first red error, perform a Full Rebuild in Packaging options if assets seem corrupted, then repackage. Misconception: assuming a successful editor test guarantees a working packaged build — always validate using the packaged logs. Closing question: after you find an error in the Output Log, what single change will you test first?

Deployment varies by target platform. For Windows, the packaged output is a folder containing an executable and associated content; you typically compress that folder into a zip for distribution or provide an installer. Before distributing, test the executable on a clean machine to confirm dependencies are present. For mobile platforms, packaging produces platform-specific bundles such as an APK for Android or an IPA for iOS; these require additional configuration for SDK paths and signing credentials. A clear example: packaging an Android build fails if the Android SDK or NDK paths are not set in Project Settings. Another area to watch is the difference between Development and Shipping builds: Development builds are larger and include debug helpers, so they are useful for diagnosing crashes on device, while Shipping builds must be signed and may require store compliance steps. A common misconception is assuming packaging is the same as deployment — packaging creates the build; deployment is the act of delivering it to users and often requires zipping, signing, or uploading to a store. Takeaway: test packaged builds on the target hardware and verify SDK and signing settings for mobile before attempting distribution.

Archiving is the practice of creating a complete, restorable snapshot of your Unreal project for long-term storage or milestone sign-off. Unlike daily version control commits that record diffs, an archive bundles everything needed to reopen and run the project later — including files you may not track in Git. A good archive captures project assets, configuration, and any local engine builds or platform-specific settings. This matters because team members, future you, or release QA may need an exact restore point that is independent from a commit history. As a result, treat version control as your primary collaboration tool and archives as periodic, complete backups that you can hand to QA or store offline. Here are three compact concepts to anchor your understanding of packaging. Packaging compiles and bundles assets, Blueprints, and code into a standalone application suitable for distribution. Cooking prepares assets for the target platform, converting them into optimized formats before packaging and reducing runtime surprises. The Pak file is a single archive that groups game content for efficient distribution and loading. Keep these concepts in mind because they explain why packaging settings and the list of included maps are both critical to a working build. If a map isn’t listed or an asset fails to cook, the packaged game may crash at runtime. These three terms are quick checks when something goes wrong: Did you cook? Did you include the maps?
